newsitem.title: UK: Gold leaps from the abyss, coffee and base metals firm.
newsitem.headline: Gold leaps from the abyss, coffee and base metals firm.

text.p: The price of gold staged a spectacular bounce on Wednesday after it fell to 3-3/4 year lows then speculative funds suddenly came in and bought it.
Gold rose almost $10 to trade above $345 an ounce after it had sunk as low as $336.50 in early European business.
The early fall extended a long decline, mainly on fears that other central banks may follow a recent Dutch example and sell bullion from their reserves.
A strong dollar added to the pressure on gold by propping the metal's value in the currencies of nations outside the United States -- when jittery speculators saw a chance to bale out.
But the dollar eased later and investment funds also decided to buy platinum, when the bullion market generally rallied.

Elsewhere in commodity markets, crude oil and grains traded within expected ranges. Coffee survived a bout of profit-taking to hold close to recent highs at values 35-40 percent higher than in early January.
New York futures for Arabica coffee climbed to fresh contract highs after opening lower on profit taking.

March Arabica futures hit a fresh contract high of 171.00 cents per pound in the rally that has already worked through to firmer retail prices in Europe and the United States and may have further to go.
"The target is probably 177.00 cents on a technical basis before serious resistance will be seen," Refco New York analyst Anne Prendergast said.

"Roasters have been buying on a just-in-time basis but are now being caught by a potential supply shock with the prospect of a low Brazilian crop this year, while the early 1996/97 crops has already been well absorbed and consumer stocks are very low," she said.
Concerns about the effect of a Colombian state workers strike which began Tuesday also fuelled bullish sentiment, analysts said.
Industrial metals also staged a modest rally and copper and aluminium ended near the day's highs on the London Metal Exchange.
The rest of the base metals were also boosted higher as short covering and speculative buying lifted sagging prices.
Aluminium ended the afternoon kerb $8 firmer at $1,555 per tonne, having snapped up from support at $1,535 early in the day.
That close above $1,550 signalled a chance for consolidation after four days of sharp falls, analysts said.
Copper trundled higher after support at the important $2,200 area held despite protracted tests, traders said.
It ended the afternoon kerb at the important $2,250 level, an increase of $38 from Tuesday, and just below the day's high of $2,555.

The dollar's rise in value of more than 7-1/2 percent since January 1, measured against a trade-weighted basket of currencies, is good news for some exporters of raw materials, on which most prices are set in dollars.
"OPEC will breathe a sigh of relief if the dollar continues to strengthen,' said Geoff Pyne, an energy economist with UBS.
The dollar rally may reduce the risk of new trade tension between the European Union and the US over export subsidies as the EU battles to stay competitive on weakening world grain markets.

A firm dollar means the EU can afford to pay lower subsidies in European currency units to make up the difference between the price at which its farmers can afford to produce and a world price set in the dollar.
